comment.value: Star formation history and stellar age from CMD fitting of two HST/ACS fields, which cover approximately 18% of the stellar mass and lie within the half-light radius; the authors note that an age gradient could make the star formation appear later than it was for the galaxy as a whole. The cumulative epochs at 11.8 and 10.0 Gyr are quoted in Section 4.5 of the paper. Those at 12.0 and 8.0 Gyr are not quoted: they were digitized from the cumulative curve in the right panel of Figure 4 (with an estimated read-off uncertainty of 0.01 in fraction) for comparison with other entries in this database that give the fractions at these times. In the same figure the 50% and 90% guide lines lie at approximately 11.7 and 10.2 Gyr, so the quoted times appear to be rounded. The cumulative curve includes minor star formation at lookback times below 8 Gyr that the authors do not consider significant. ageStellar is the mean age of the main star formation peak (Table 3), whose fitted width of 0.9 Gyr includes the age resolution of the method (0.57 Gyr for a mock population of negligible width and age 12 Gyr). CMD fitting gives a metallicity distribution centered on [Z/H]=-1.86 with width 0.16 dex, comparable to the 0.15 dex found for M92 with the same method. The paper derives a present-day stellar mass of (4.03+/-1.16)e5 Msun, the average of M/L=1.6 applied to L_V=2.3e5 Lsun and the integrated star formation history corrected for recycling; massStellar instead retains M/L=1 for comparability with other entries.

comment.value: Binary w/NGC 147? Star formation history is from CMD fitting which reaches the oldest main sequence turnoff (Table 3 of Savino et al. 2025), with statistical and systematic uncertainties combined. It comes from one HST/ACS field, about 6.6 arcminutes from the center, which contains only about 2% of the total light. The authors note that NGC 185 has significant stellar population gradients and lies off the relation between median age and luminosity, so this may not represent the whole galaxy. Ventura et al. (2026; arXiv:2611.06547) derive a later history from the same data by fitting evolved stars (horizontal branch, red clump, RGB and AGB): 50%, 75% and 90% of stars formed by 11.1, 8.9 and 6.6 Gyr ago, read from the plotted data of their Figure 8, which agrees with their text (more than 11 Gyr, and slightly below 7 Gyr). That history is not used here because it depends on the assumed RGB mass loss and on a single metallicity (Z=0.002) for the old stars, gives no uncertainties on these epochs, and lies outside the uncertainties of Savino et al. Savino et al. fit the turnoff directly, in the same way for all of their M31 satellites, and agree with Geha et al. (2015). Ventura et al. report that their history agrees better with the long-period variable result of Hamedani Golshan et al. (2017) and with the relation between N_AGB/N_RGB and T90, and also find an average RGB mass loss of 0.22 +/- 0.01 Msun and N_AGB/N_RGB of about 0.08.
